slides.title: Each lever changes a different part of the system
slides.text: Four ways to change what a model does Each lever changes a different part of the system Prompt Changes the instructions. Minutes to try, read again on every request. Retrieve Changes what the model is shown: a table, a document, a record. Tune Changes the weights, from your examples. Days of work, then no extra tokens. Distil Tuning whose examples come from a larger model. Order of cost. Try them left to right. Each one you skip is a cheaper fix you never tested.

slides.title: Tuning changes behaviour more than knowledge
slides.text: What tuning is good at Tuning changes behaviour more than knowledge Tuning teaches well a format, exactly and every time which tool to choose when to stop and hand over to a person a register, a language, a house style Tuning teaches badly facts that change: a code table, a fee, a deadline facts seen once in the training set anything you must be able to correct tomorrow A fact in the weights cannot be edited, cited or dated. A fact in the context can.

slides.title: Small models suit narrow tasks, not multi-step work
slides.text: Where a small model belongs Small models suit narrow tasks, not multi-step work A small tuned model fits It does not fit One request in, one structured answer out A plan of several steps that depend on each other A fixed set of tools and fields Tools it has never seen Thousands of similar requests Rare requests that each need judgement An answer a program can check An answer only an expert can check Qayd is on the left. One request, one of five tools, fields a schema can verify. The rare and the odd go to the registry desk through escalate_to_staff.

slides.title: A weak prompt flatters tuning
slides.text: The most common false result in fine-tuning A weak prompt flatters tuning "Our tuned model went from 27 to 85" compares a week of work with one careless sentence Half of that gain may be available in an afternoon, with no training at all The honest comparison is against the best prompt you could write What the baseline is for It is the number the adapter must beat on Day 4. If the adapter cannot beat a good prompt on the same model, the project ends here, cheaply.

slides.title: One change at a time, each scored on the same 100 requests
slides.text: Method One change at a time, each scored on the same 100 requests v0 one sentence → v1 schema hints → v2 the code table → v3 the rules → v4 four examples Each change targets a class. Schema hints: format. The table: knowledge. Rules and examples: behaviour, as far as words can reach it.

slides.title: A schema hint tells the model what a call looks like
slides.text: Version 1 A schema hint tells the model what a call looks like Answer with exactly one tool call and nothing else, in this form: <tool_call> {"name": "<tool>", "arguments": {...}} </tool_call> Tools: create_membership(company_name, cr_number, city, activity_code) … escalate_to_staff(reason) cr_number is 10 Western digits (convert Arabic-Indic digits). company_name is copied as written. city is the English name. The wrapperThe interfaceHow to write each field

slides.title: A baseline is three things that never change again
slides.text: What "frozen" means A baseline is three things that never change again The instructions Identified by a hash of their text and examples. One edited sentence is a new baseline. The set The same file of requests, by name and by content. The score Right answers, n, and the interval. Recorded with the model's name and the day. {"prompt_sha256": "bdf86a63…", "n": 100, "correct": 67, "accuracy": 0.67, "interval": [0.573, 0.754], "set": "data/requests_100.jsonl"}

slides.title: Licences and terms of open-weight models
slides.text: Session 3 Licences and terms of open-weight models Distinguish permission to adapt, to deploy and to distribute in a model licence Find conditions that depend on who deploys and for what Record which candidate models the chamber may adapt and deploy 03

slides.title: "Open weights" means you can download it, not what you may do with it
slides.text: Before any training "Open weights" means you can download it, not what you may do with it Every model on the Hub has a licence file. The tag on the card is a label someone typed Licences differ on purpose, on revenue, on field of use and on what you pass on The check costs an hour before training and a project after deployment Who decides You find the clause and the fact it depends on. Zakariya Al-Mousa, the chamber's counsel, decides. "Ask counsel" is a valid entry in your table.

slides.title: Adapt, deploy and distribute are three separate permissions
slides.text: Read a licence with three questions Adapt, deploy and distribute are three separate permissions Adapt Fine-tune it. The result is a derivative work in most licences. Deploy Run it in a service. Here licences ask for what purpose and by whom. Distribute Give the weights or the adapter to someone else. Conditions travel with it. The chamber's plan needs all three: tune on its requests, run inside a service members pay fees for, give the adapter to two sister chambers.

slides.title: Three candidate models, three kinds of licence
slides.text: Lab 1.3 · read on 15 November 2026 Three candidate models, three kinds of licence Model Licence The clause that decides Qwen3-0.6B Apache License 2.0 Grants derivative works and redistribution; no clause on purpose or revenue LFM3-1.7B LFM Open License v1.0 Commercial use is licensed only below USD 10 million of annual revenue Command R7B Arabic CC BY-NC 4.0, gated Every right is for non-commercial purposes; more conditions may sit behind the gate Names are examples, not endorsements. The slot matters: a permissive licence, one that depends on who you are, one that depends on what for.

slides.title: Two conditions turn on facts about the chamber
slides.text: A licence table without facts is an opinion Two conditions turn on facts about the chamber The revenue threshold The chamber's annual revenue is SAR 62 million, which is USD 16.5 million: above the threshold. Its use is licensed only if it is not "commercial use". The purpose The chamber is a non-profit body, and its service charges fees. Is that "primarily intended for commercial advantage or monetary compensation"? The text does not say. Write the question down now. "Ask" in the table, with the clause and the fact, is a result. Finding out after deployment is not.

slides.title: Read the text, record the day, look for a second document
slides.text: Three habits Read the text, record the day, look for a second document The text, not the tag. Open the licence file in the repository; a card can say "other" and hide everything The day you read it. A later release of the same family can carry different terms A second document. An acceptable-use policy, or conditions on a gated page, bind you as well The teacher too. On Day 3 a larger model writes your training labels: its terms on using outputs to train another model belong in the same table

slides.title: The decision memo carries one licence line
slides.text: What Maysoon reads The decision memo carries one licence line WeakAll three models are open source, so licensing is not a concern. UsableTake Qwen3-0.6B forward: Apache License 2.0, sections 2 and 4, allows adapting, deploying and passing on the adapter with the licence text and a notice of changes. LFM3-1.7B needs counsel's answer on section 5: the chamber is above the revenue threshold.

slides.title: May we deploy it?
slides.text: Checkpoint May we deploy it? A model's licence allows commercial use only to organisations with annual revenue under USD 10 million. The chamber's revenue is above that, and its registration service charges fees. What goes in the "deploy" column? Yes: the weights are open, so use is free Yes: a chamber is a non-profit body, so the limit cannot apply Yes, once the model is fine-tuned, because the adapter is ours Ask: counsel must decide whether a fee-charging service is commercial use

slides.title: A hosted model costs per token; an owned accelerator costs per month
slides.text: Two ways to pay for a model A hosted model costs per token; an owned accelerator costs per month Hosted a price per million input and output tokens cost grows with volume, starts at zero the request leaves your servers Owned purchase over its useful life, power, an engineer's hours the same cost at one request or a million the request stays where you put the machine Cost per thousand requests is the unit that makes them comparable, and for the owned machine it depends entirely on volume.

slides.title: A prompted request is mostly instructions
slides.text: Lab 1.4 · measured on the 100 requests A prompted request is mostly instructions 623 input tokens, prompted: instructions, table, rules, examples and the request 30 input tokens, tuned: the request alone 33 output tokens: one tool call Counts are the lab's rough estimate (four characters of English, two and a half of Arabic to a token). A provider's own count replaces them.

slides.title: At the chamber's volume the hosted model is far cheaper
slides.text: Lab 1.4 · prices read on 15 November 2026 At the chamber's volume the hosted model is far cheaper Option SAR per 1,000 requests Where a request is processed Large hosted model 0.52 The provider's servers Tuned small model, own accelerator 141.38 The chamber's own servers Do not soften this. SAR 5,655 a month for the machine, 40,000 requests a month. Break-even is about 11 million requests a month: 274 times the chamber's volume.

slides.title: Cost argues for the hosted model; placement rules it out
slides.text: What actually decides Cost argues for the hosted model; placement rules it out A request names an owner, a mobile number, sometimes an identity number: personal data The chamber classifies registration requests as Restricted Its requirement: they are processed on its own servers The honest sentence for the memo "The chamber pays a premium of about SAR 141 per thousand requests to keep members' data on its own servers. This is the premium, and this is why it is worth paying."

slides.title: Tuning is paid once; serving is paid every month
slides.text: Three costs, three shapes Tuning is paid once; serving is paid every month Cost Shape In the case Tuning Once per version of the adapter SAR 13,260: 60 engineer hours and 10 GPU hours Serving Every month, whatever the volume SAR 5,655 Per request Serving divided by volume SAR 0.14 at 40,000 requests a month Tuning is paid back in quality, not money. A prompted and a tuned small model cost the same to serve on the same machine. And the engineer costs more than the GPU.

slides.title: The volume doubles
slides.text: Checkpoint The volume doubles The chamber's requests double to 80,000 a month. The accelerator still has spare capacity. What happens to the cost per thousand requests? Both options stay the same Hosted stays the same; the owned accelerator's halves Hosted halves; the owned accelerator's stays the same Both double

slides.text: The raw material A trace is a request, the model's answer and what a person did next request نريد التجديد لمدة سنة واحدة. سجلنا التجاري 4067281583. Qayd {"name": "renew_membership", "arguments": {"cr_number": "4067281583", "years": 2}} registry desk status: corrected correction {"name": "renew_membership", "arguments": {"cr_number": "4067281583", "years": 1}} The request asks for one year (سنة واحدة). slides.title: Accepted, corrected, abandoned: three statuses, three kinds of label
slides.text: What label does a trace carry? Accepted, corrected, abandoned: three statuses, three kinds of label Status Traces The label What it can teach Accepted 342 Qayd's own output The format, again. Nothing about its failures Corrected 123 The desk's call The behaviour Qayd lacks Abandoned 35 None Nothing, until someone labels it Abandoned traces are not random. The desk gave up on the hardest requests. Leaving them out makes the tuning set easier than production.

slides.title: "Accepted" means nobody objected, not that the call was right
slides.text: The first trap "Accepted" means nobody objected, not that the call was right 8 of 342 accepted traces carry a wrong call (the generator's answer key) A rule check finds 2 of them: the number in the call is not in the request The other 6 pass every check: valid, plausible, wrong In your own project there is no answer key: only an audit of a sample tells you the rate

slides.title: A correction is typed by a person at a busy desk
slides.text: The second trap A correction is typed by a person at a busy desk What the desk typed What the registry says "cr_number": "403158269" not 10 Western digits "city": "الطائف" a value outside the list: the interface takes "Taif" "cr_number": "٤٠٥٠٥٢٢٦٨٧" not 10 Western digits Validate every label against the tool interface. 12 of the 123 corrections are rejected. A label the tool would refuse is not a label.

slides.text: Session 2 Teacher generation and verifier filtering Generate labels with a larger model under frozen instructions Filter teacher outputs with schema checks and rule checks Measure yield and estimate the errors a verifier lets through 02

slides.title: A larger model can label requests nobody corrected
slides.text: Labels for what the desk never saw A larger model can label requests nobody corrected The pilot left 900 requests with no label at all On Day 1 the larger model was right on 94 in 100 with the frozen instructions Its labels are cheap, fast and in volume, where staff time is none of the three The price It is wrong on about 6 in 100, and whatever enters the set is what the student learns. A teacher needs a verifier.

slides.title: Same output format as the student, and only data that may leave
slides.text: Two conditions before you call the teacher Same output format as the student, and only data that may leave Format The teacher gets the frozen instructions and examples. Its label must be the exact text the student has to produce, or the student learns someone else's format. Placement The pool in the lab is synthetic. Real members' requests are Restricted: a hosted teacher may not see them. Run the teacher on your own servers, or label masked and synthetic requests only. The teacher's terms count too. Its licence and its provider's conditions on training another model with its outputs belong in yesterday's licence table.

slides.title: A verifier has two layers: the schema, then rules against the request
slides.text: What stands between the teacher and the set A verifier has two layers: the schema, then rules against the request Teacher output 300 → Schema would the registry accept it? 6 rejected → Rules does it agree with the request? 1 rejected → Kept 293 A schema knows the interface, not the request. "cr_number": "4000000000" is a valid argument and an invention. Only a rule that reads the request can tell.

slides.title: A rule check compares the call with the text it claims to answer
slides.text: Lab 2.2 · task 3 A rule check compares the call with the text it claims to answer numbers = CR.findall(C.western_digits(text)) # numbers the request contains args = call["arguments"] if "cr_number" in args and args["cr_number"] not in numbers: errors.append("the registration number is not in the request") if call["name"] == "escalate_to_staff" and args.get("reason") == "missing_cr" and numbers: errors.append("escalated as missing although the request gives a number") if call["name"] == "create_membership" and args.get("company_name", "") not in text: errors.append("the company name is not in the request")

slides.text: What passes Valid, consistent with the request, and wrong The teacher's error Schema Rules Takes the partner's registration number passes passes: the number is in the request Renews where a certificate was asked for passes passes Writes two years for "one year" passes passes Invents a registration number passes caught Answers in prose caught

slides.title: The model never sees your messages: it sees one string
slides.text: What the model actually reads The model never sees your messages: it sees one string <|im_start|>user نأمل إرسال شهادة العضوية للسجل التجاري 4029184372.<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant <tool_call> {"name": "issue_certificate", "arguments": {"cr_number": "4029184372", "kind": "membership"}} </tool_call><|im_end|> Role markers, an end-of-turn token, a wrapper for the call. Every one of these is a convention of this model, written in its template.

slides.title: The chat template is part of the model
slides.text: The durable idea The chat template is part of the model The base model was trained on strings in exactly this shape Your adapter will be served strings in exactly this shape So train on strings in exactly this shape: use the template, do not rewrite it What goes wrong A hand-written renderer trains "fine": the loss falls, because the model learns whatever text it is given. The fault shows in production, as a format nobody sends.

slides.title: The server sends the prompt; training adds the answer
slides.text: Two renderings of one example The server sends the prompt; training adds the answer Prompt add_generation_prompt=True: the request, then the marker that opens the assistant's turn. The model writes what follows. Full The whole conversation, the assistant's turn and its end-of-turn token included. The full text must start with the prompt, character for character. That prefix property is what makes the label mask possible: everything up to the end of the prompt is context, everything after it is the target.

slides.title: Two model families, two ways to write the same call
slides.text: Tool-call formats Two model families, two ways to write the same call Qwen3: JSON in tags <tool_call> {"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Paris"}} </tool_call> LFM3: an XML form in tags <tool_call> <function=get_weather> <parameter=city> Paris </parameter> </function> </tool_call> Change the base model and the tuning set must be rendered again. Store messages, never rendered strings.

slides.title: Three faults that train "fine" and fail in service
slides.text: Lab 2.3 Three faults that train "fine" and fail in service 1 · The turn never ends No end-of-turn token after the answer. The adapter never learns to stop and writes to the token limit on every request. 2 · A foreign call format str(call): single quotes, no tags. The model is taught the Python-dictionary failure of Lab 1.1. 3 · Loss on everything Labels equal to the input. A third of the signal goes into predicting members' requests instead of the answer.

slides.title: The loss is taken on the assistant's turn only
slides.text: Fault 3, fixed The loss is taken on the assistant's turn only prompt_ids = tok(prompt, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"] full_ids = tok(full, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"] labels = [-100] * len(prompt_ids) + full_ids[len(prompt_ids):] # ignored by the loss the tool call and the end of turn Why it matters beyond efficiency. A model trained to predict requests is trained to reproduce what members wrote. Masking the prompt is also a data-protection measure.

slides.title: Encode, decode, compare: does the text survive the tokeniser?
slides.text: The check people skip Encode, decode, compare: does the text survive the tokeniser? writtenالرد على owner289@member.example أو الاتصال على 0509022407. decodedالرد على owner289<|unk|>member.example أو الاتصال على 0509022407. The course tokeniser has no token for the @ sign. Masking removes the address before the tokeniser sees it (Lab 2.4), and the lab's fixed renderer round-trips 50 of 50 masked examples.

slides.title: It answers, and then it keeps writing
slides.text: Checkpoint It answers, and then it keeps writing A freshly tuned adapter produces the correct tool call and then continues with more calls and stray text until the token limit. The base model never did this. Where do you look first? The rendered training text: is there an end-of-turn token after the assistant's answer? The learning rate: it was too high The server: raise the stop-token limit The tuning set: it needs more examples

slides.title: Duplicates inflate, leaks flatter, personal data does not belong in weights
slides.text: What a loss curve will never show Duplicates inflate, leaks flatter, personal data does not belong in weights Near-duplicates The same request, sent twice with "Hello" in front. The set looks larger than it is, and one member's wording is over-weighted. Test-set overlap A test request in the tuning set. Every score on Day 4 would be too high, by an unknown amount. Personal data Names, mobile numbers, identity numbers in free text. Not needed to choose a tool, and a model can reproduce what it was trained on.

slides.title: Near-duplicate: one text's three-word runs are contained in the other's
slides.text: A rule you can state in one sentence Near-duplicate: one text's three-word runs are contained in the other's keptKindly extend the membership of CR 4013583134 by 1 year. removedKindly extend the membership of CR 4013583134 by 1 year. Regards. Normalise: lower case, Western digits, no punctuation Compare runs of three words; containment = shared runs divided by the smaller set Near-duplicate at 0.9 or more, compared only within the same registration number

slides.title: At 0.8 the rule merged two different requests
slides.text: A threshold is a decision, and it has a cost At 0.8 the rule merged two different requests kept at 0.8نرجو إرسال قائمة بجميع الأعضاء العاملين في الاستشارات. removed at 0.8نرجو إرسال قائمة بجميع الأعضاء العاملين في الأجهزة الطبية. Two short requests that differ only in the activity they ask about: five of the six word runs of the shorter one are shared. At 0.8 they count as one; at 0.9 both stay. The lower threshold removed 82 rows, the higher one 67. Read what a threshold removes before you accept it. Print ten removed pairs; if one is not a duplicate, the threshold is wrong for your data.

slides.title: A leak is removed; a template collision is kept and counted
slides.text: Decontamination A leak is removed; a template collision is kept and counted Leak Template collision What it is A near-copy of a test request about the same registration number A short request with no number that many members write alike Example "We are Al-Salam Supplies Est. from Dammam … CR 4001995900" "We need a membership certificate as soon as possible." In the lab 18 removed 31 kept Why A test case inside the training data Removing it would delete a kind of request from training

CR number 4042480051. baseCALL issue_certificate cr_number=4042480051 kind=membership wanted<tool_call> {"name": "issue_certificate", "arguments": {"cr_number": "4042480051", "kind": "membership"}} </tool_call> On the 120 validation requests the base produces 0 valid calls. slides.title: Full fine-tuning moves every weight, and keeps a copy per task
slides.text: Why not train everything? Full fine-tuning moves every weight, and keeps a copy per task Gradients and optimiser state for every parameter: several times the memory of the weights One full copy of the model for each task you tune Every weight can move, so everything the base knew can be disturbed The adapter's bet The change a task needs is small and has structure. Freeze the base; learn only a low-rank correction to a few of its matrices.

slides.title: W stays frozen; the adapter adds B·A beside it
slides.text: Low-rank adaptation W stays frozen; the adapter adds B·A beside it W d_out × d_in, frozen + B d_out × r, starts at zero · A r × d_in, starts random × alpha / r a fixed scale Parameters added to one matrix: r × (d_in + d_out) B starts at zero, so at step 0 the adapted model is the base Which matrices get an adapter is a setting: today, the query and value projections of every attention layer

slides.title: 1.6% of the parameters train
slides.text: Lab 3.1 · task 1 1.6% of the parameters train 1,001,728 parameters in the course model, all frozen 16,384 in a rank-8 adapter on 8 matrices 68 KB the adapter on disk: the only file you ship per task Count before you train. If the trainable share is not what you expect, the adapter is on the wrong modules, or the base is not frozen.

slides.title: The whole training loop fits on a slide
slides.text: tuning.train, in essence The whole training loop fits on a slide params = [p for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad] # the adapter only opt = torch.optim.AdamW(params, lr=lr) for step in range(steps): x, labels, mask = next_batch() # rendered with the template; labels masked on the prompt for group in opt.param_groups: group["lr"] = lr * schedule(step) # warm-up, then cosine decay loss = model(input_ids=x, attention_mask=mask, labels=labels).loss loss.backward() torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(params, 1.0) opt.step(); opt.zero_grad() if (step + 1) % 25 == 0: log(step, loss, loss_on(model, validation))

slides.title: Whether a model fits is arithmetic: parameters times bits
slides.text: Do this before you rent anything Whether a model fits is arithmetic: parameters times bits Parameters 16 bits 4 bits 0.6 billion 1.1 GB 0.3 GB 1.7 billion 3.2 GB 0.8 GB 7 billion 13.0 GB 3.5 GB 27 billion 50.3 GB 13.4 GB Weights only. 16 bits is two bytes a weight. 4 bits is half a byte, plus here one 16-bit scale for every block of 64 weights.

slides.title: The weights are the floor; training adds three things on top
slides.text: Why "it fits" is not the end of it The weights are the floor; training adds three things on top Activations Kept for every token of every example in the batch, at every layer, for the backward pass. Grows with batch size × sequence length. Adapter gradients Small: only A and B have them. Optimiser state Two more numbers for each trainable parameter with AdamW. Small for the same reason. Out of memory with weights that fit? Lower the batch size or the maximum length first. Gradient accumulation keeps the effective batch.

slides.title: A 4-bit weight is one of 16 levels, times the scale of its block
slides.text: Lab 3.2 · task 1 A 4-bit weight is one of 16 levels, times the scale of its block scale = block.abs().max() # one number kept per block of 64 weights nearest = (block / scale - levels).abs().argmin() # index of the closest of 16 levels: 4 bits rounded = levels[nearest] * scale # what the model computes with The 16 levels are not evenly spaced: they are denser near zero, where most weights of a trained network lie (the NF4 type) Rounding is an error added to every weight. Whether it matters is an empirical question, per model and per task

slides.title: The base is rounded and frozen; the adapter trains in full precision
slides.text: Training on a quantised base The base is rounded and frozen; the adapter trains in full precision 4-bit base frozen, rounded + Adapter full precision, trainable → Loss on the assistant's turn Gradients pass through the rounded weights to the adapter; the rounded weights never change The adapter learns the task and part of what rounding lost So the adapter belongs to its base at that precision: serve it on the base it was trained on

slides.text: Lab 3.2 · task 4 The same adapter on two bases 16-bit base 4-bit base Base weights (course model) 1.91 MB 0.85 MB Untrained, valid calls of 120 0 0 Final validation loss 0.0124 0.0125 Validation requests right, of 120 85 87 Why not 4 to 1? slides.text: Three questions before you distil Distillation needs a better teacher, usable outputs and data that may be sent Is the teacher better? On this behaviour, measured on the same requests (Lab 1.1). A teacher that fails the same way has nothing to teach. May its outputs train a model? The licence of an open-weight teacher, or the terms of a hosted one. Read them as you read the student's licence on Day 1. May the requests reach it? Restricted requests may not go to a hosted teacher. Run the teacher on your own servers, or label synthetic and masked requests.

slides.text: Why two scores are not enough The same two scores can hide very different disagreements A right B right Only A right Only B right Case 1 380 372 8 0 Case 2 380 372 40 32 Case 1: every disagreement goes one way. slides.title: A paired difference is +1, 0 or −1 on each request
slides.text: Lab 4.1 · task 2 A paired difference is +1, 0 or −1 on each request d = [a_right - b_right for a_right, b_right in zip(a, b)] # +1, 0 or -1 per request difference = sum(d) / len(d) # the difference in accuracy means = sorted(sum(random.choices(d, k=len(d))) / len(d) # resample the requests, for _ in range(2000)) # two thousand times low, high = means[50], means[1949] # the middle 95% Requests that both systems get right, or both get wrong, contribute 0: difficulty cancels The interval comes from the disagreements. Zero inside it: no difference shown

slides.title: Write what the interval supports, and nothing more
slides.text: Lab 4.1 · task 4 Write what the interval supports, and nothing more Interval above zero "A is better than B on requests like these." Say how much, with the interval. Interval below zero "B is better than A." The same sentence, the other way. Zero inside "No difference shown." Not "they are equal": a larger test set might show one. "On requests like these" is part of every sentence. The test set is synthetic and comes from the same generator as the tuning set; production requests will be less tidy.

slides.title: The adapter is added to shared weights, for every input

slides.title: Write the release rule before you see the next model's numbers
slides.text: Lab 4.2 · stretch Write the release rule before you see the next model's numbers def release_blocked(refused, of, general_right, general_of, base_general): reasons = [] if refused < of: reasons.append("a request for personal data was not refused: any is too many") if general_right < 0.95 * base_general: reasons.append("the general check fell by more than 5%") return reasons A regression check finds only the regressions someone thought to test for. 200 items and 60 requests are a floor. The model card says what was checked, so that a reader can see what was not.

slides.title: Requests that arrive together share each forward pass
slides.text: Where throughput comes from Requests that arrive together share each forward pass A model computes a batch of requests in little more time than one The server collects what is waiting and answers it together, each row with its own adapter More requests in flight: larger batches, more answers per second, and a longer wait for each In the teaching server Up to 16 requests, or whatever arrived within 10 milliseconds, form a batch. Production servers refill the batch continuously, token by token.

slides.title: A member who waits is a percentile, not a mean
slides.text: How to read a latency column A member who waits is a percentile, not a mean p50 Half of the answers arrive within this time. The typical member. p95 One answer in twenty takes longer. The number a service level is written on. p99 One in a hundred. At 40,000 requests a month, 400 members. Capacity is throughput under a latency target. "It handles N requests a second" means nothing until it says at which percentile, within how many milliseconds, with no failures.
